chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Asbaat, with an unbroken chain, said:
Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) wrote to Ibn Abbas: 'Having said that,'
what makes a person happy is what he did not miss, and grieves for what he never could have attained, ever.
And if you strive, let your joy be in what you have sent forward of righteous deeds, or judgment, or speech.
And let your regret be regarding what you have neglected from that.
And leave what has passed from the world, and do not grieve much over it.
And what has befallen you of it, do not delight in it with excessive joy.
And let your concern be for what comes after death.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (title for Imam Ali)

ai.seo_question: How should a Muslim balance joy and grief regarding worldly得失 according to Imam Ali's letter to Ibn Abbas?
ai.summary: This letter from Imam Ali (as) to Ibn Abbas establishes a psychological framework for spiritual resilience, distinguishing between internal agency (one's own deeds) and external fate (worldly gains/losses). It reflects the Shia emphasis on *tawakkul* combined with active effort, urging the believer to anchor their emotional state in the permanence of the afterlife rather than the transience of worldly fluctuations.

en.hubeali: H 14775 – A number of our companions, from Sahl Bin Ziyad, from Ali Bin Asbaat with an unbroken chain, said:
Amir-ul-Momineenasws wrote to Ibn Abbas: ‘Having said that,
what has made the person happy is what he did not miss, and grieved for what he never could have got, ever.
The efforts that you have made should make you happy with what you have sent forward from the righteous deeds, or Judgement, or speech,
and it is to your regret regarding what you have neglected from that.
And leave what you have missed from the world and do not grieve a lot for it.
And what you have got from it, do not enjoy in its delight,
but ponder over what comes after the death.
